content.title: About
content.content: A quesadilla is a traditional Mexican dish consisting of a thin corn or flour tortilla filled with melted cheese and meat (beef or pork), then toasted until golden and crispy. It is served hot, often accompanied by salsa, guacamole, and sour cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Quesadillas originated in central Mexico long before European colonization, using native varieties of corn.
The word “quesadilla” derives from the Spanish “queso,” meaning cheese.
In the United States, quesadillas surged in popularity during the 1990s alongside the rise of Mexican cuisine.
While the classic version contains only cheese, modern fillings include vegetables, beans, and various meats.
Quesadillas are frequently served as “Mexican tacos” when cut into triangular wedges.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef or pork provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: Red meat is a good source of heme iron and zinc, which support immune function and metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Melted cheese adds calcium that contributes to bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and cheese are rich in B12, B6, and niacin, important for energy production.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: When made with a flour tortilla, the carbohydrate load remains moderate, fitting a moderately low‑carb diet.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Cheese and fatty meat can raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese often contains a lot of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: Individuals with milk protein allergy or lactose intolerance should choose dairy‑free cheese alternatives.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor pathogenic bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C (160 °F).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the quesadilla hot, cut into wedges. Pair with salsa, guacamole, sour cream, or fresh cilantro. For a lighter version, use a whole‑grain tortilla and reduced‑fat cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked quesadillas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For freezing, wrap tightly in plastic film and aluminum foil; keep up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to ensure the filling is hot throughout.
